## Introduction

In class we built support vector machines one idea at a time: a **hyperplane**
that separates two classes, the **maximal margin classifier** that picks the
widest such hyperplane, the **soft margin** that tolerates some violations, and
**kernels** that bend the boundary. This lab has four parts:

1. **See the ideas.** Simulated data with sliders — move a hyperplane by hand,
   push support vectors around, turn the cost dial, switch kernels.
2. **The tumor example from the slides.** Real biopsy data, the same two
   features (cell size and cell shape uniformity), then all nine.
3. **More than two classes.** Iris, three species, one-versus-one.
4. **Variable selection for classification.** Thirty correlated tumor features:
   ordinary logistic regression breaks, and the lasso picks a handful.

Every code cell runs live in your browser via webR — no local R install
needed. Packages and data load once when the page opens; give it a few seconds
on first load.

**Two kinds of cells.** The **interactive cells** (the ones with sliders above
them) run on their own and re-run every time you move a slider — just play.
Every other cell runs when you click **Run Code**; run those in order from the
top of each part, because later cells use objects made by earlier ones.

## A warning about C before we start

The slides (and ISLR) write the soft margin with a **budget** $C$:

$$\sum_{i=1}^n \epsilon_i \le C .$$

A **large** budget means *more* tolerance for points on the wrong side of the
margin — a wider margin.

Every R package we use (`kernlab`, `e1071`, `caret`) instead uses a **cost**
`C`: the price paid per unit of violation. A **large** cost means *less*
tolerance — a narrower margin. The two run in **opposite directions**:

| | slides / ISLR budget $C$ | software cost `C` |
|---|---|---|
| wider margin, more violations, more support vectors | large | small |
| narrower margin, fewer violations, fewer support vectors | small | large |

Everything in this lab uses the software meaning. When you read `C = 100`
below, think "violations are expensive", not "a big budget".

We use `kernlab::ksvm()` directly for the pictures in Part 1 and
`caret::train()` for the real-data fits, following
[Lab 5](../../05-classification-1/code/class5_lab1.html): `method =
"svmLinear"`, `"svmPoly"`, and `"svmRadial"` all call `kernlab` underneath.

# Part 1 — Seeing the ideas

## 1.1 A hyperplane is just a sign

With $p = 2$ features a hyperplane is a line,
$f(X) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_1 + \beta_2 X_2 = 0$. The slides normalize
$\beta_1^2 + \beta_2^2 = 1$; we build that in by writing
$\beta_1 = \cos\theta$, $\beta_2 = \sin\theta$, so the two sliders below are the
**direction** of the normal vector (the angle $\theta$) and the **offset**
$\beta_0$.

The shading shows the sign of $f(X)$. A point with label $y_i = \pm 1$ is on
the correct side when $y_i f(x_i) > 0$. When every point is on the correct
side, you have a **separating hyperplane**, and — because
$\beta_1^2 + \beta_2^2 = 1$ — the smallest $y_i f(x_i)$ is the **margin** $M$:
the distance from the line to the closest point.

**Your job:** find a separating hyperplane, then make $M$ as large as you can.
The title tells you the best achievable value.

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof theta = Inputs.range([0, 355], {value: 0, step: 5, label: "angle θ (degrees)"})
viewof beta0 = Inputs.range([-5, 5], {value: -2, step: 0.05, label: "offset β₀"})
```

```{webr}
#| autorun: true
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 6
#| input:
#|   - theta
#|   - beta0
library(ggplot2)

# Two well-separated clouds; y = -1 (lower left) and y = +1 (upper right)
set.seed(6)
n <- 20
sep <- data.frame(X1 = c(rnorm(n, 1, 0.5), rnorm(n, 3, 0.5)),
                  X2 = c(rnorm(n, 1, 0.5), rnorm(n, 3, 0.5)),
                  y  = rep(c(-1, 1), each = n))

# The hyperplane you chose (beta1^2 + beta2^2 = 1)
b1 <- cos(theta * pi / 180)
b2 <- sin(theta * pi / 180)
f  <- beta0 + b1 * sep$X1 + b2 * sep$X2
n_wrong <- sum(sep$y * f <= 0)
M <- min(sep$y * f)

grid <- expand.grid(X1 = seq(-0.5, 4.5, length.out = 120),
                     X2 = seq(-0.5, 4.5, length.out = 120))
grid$f <- beta0 + b1 * grid$X1 + b2 * grid$X2

headline <- if (n_wrong == 0) {
  sprintf("Separating hyperplane!  Your margin M = %.2f  (best possible: 0.49)", M)
} else {
  sprintf("%d point(s) on the wrong side (circled)  —  keep going", n_wrong)
}

ggplot() +
  geom_raster(data = grid, aes(X1, X2, fill = f > 0), alpha = 0.25) +
  geom_contour(data = grid, aes(X1, X2, z = f), breaks = 0, colour = "black",
               linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(data = sep, aes(X1, X2, colour = factor(y)), size = 3) +
  geom_point(data = sep[sep$y * f <= 0, ], aes(X1, X2), shape = 21,
             size = 7, stroke = 1.2) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(`FALSE` = "#3B4992", `TRUE` = "#EE0000"),
                    labels = c("f(X) < 0", "f(X) > 0"), name = NULL) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(`-1` = "#3B4992", `1` = "#EE0000"),
                      labels = c("y = -1", "y = +1"), name = NULL) +
  coord_equal(xlim = c(-0.5, 4.5), ylim = c(-0.5, 4.5), expand = FALSE) +
  labs(title = headline) +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

Notice how many different lines separate these two clouds — infinitely many.
Separation alone does not pick a classifier; that is why we ask for the one
with the **largest margin**. (Hint if you are stuck: the best angle is about
40° and the best offset about −2.75.)

## 1.2 The maximal margin classifier and its support vectors

`ksvm()` with a linear kernel and a huge cost (`C = 10000`, so no violations
are affordable) finds the maximal margin hyperplane for us. The solid line is
the hyperplane; the dashed lines are the margins; circled points are the
**support vectors**.

The slides claim the support vectors are the only points that matter. Test
it: pick a point and slide it **away from** (positive) or **toward**
(negative) the boundary. The grey line is the original hyperplane for
comparison.

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof which_point = Inputs.radio(["a support vector", "a point far from the margin"], {value: "a support vector", label: "Move"})
viewof shift = Inputs.range([-0.4, 1.5], {value: 0, step: 0.05, label: "distance moved"})
```

```{webr}
#| autorun: true
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 6
#| input:
#|   - which_point
#|   - shift
library(ggplot2)
library(kernlab)

set.seed(6)
n <- 20
sep <- data.frame(X1 = c(rnorm(n, 1, 0.5), rnorm(n, 3, 0.5)),
                  X2 = c(rnorm(n, 1, 0.5), rnorm(n, 3, 0.5)),
                  y  = factor(rep(c(-1, 1), each = n)))

fit_mmc <- function(d) {
  ksvm(y ~ X1 + X2, data = d, kernel = "vanilladot", kpar = list(),
       C = 10000, scaled = FALSE)
}
margin_M <- function(m) {                       # M = 1 / ||beta||
  w <- colSums(coef(m)[[1]] * xmatrix(m)[[1]])
  1 / sqrt(sum(w^2))
}

m0 <- fit_mmc(sep)
w0 <- colSums(coef(m0)[[1]] * xmatrix(m0)[[1]])
u  <- w0 / sqrt(sum(w0^2))                       # unit normal to the hyperplane
f0 <- predict(m0, sep, type = "decision")[, 1]

# Choose the point: the first support vector, or the point farthest from the line
i <- if (which_point == "a support vector") alphaindex(m0)[[1]][1] else which.max(abs(f0))

# Move it along the normal: positive = away from the boundary
moved <- sep
moved[i, c("X1", "X2")] <- sep[i, c("X1", "X2")] + shift * sign(f0[i]) * u
m1 <- fit_mmc(moved)

grid <- expand.grid(X1 = seq(-0.5, 4.5, length.out = 150),
                    X2 = seq(-0.5, 4.5, length.out = 150))
grid$f0 <- predict(m0, grid, type = "decision")[, 1]
grid$f1 <- predict(m1, grid, type = "decision")[, 1]
sv <- moved[alphaindex(m1)[[1]], ]

ggplot() +
  geom_contour(data = grid, aes(X1, X2, z = f0), breaks = 0,
               colour = "grey60", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_contour(data = grid, aes(X1, X2, z = f1), breaks = 0,
               colour = "black", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_contour(data = grid, aes(X1, X2, z = f1), breaks = c(-1, 1),
               colour = "black", linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_point(data = moved, aes(X1, X2, colour = y), size = 3) +
  geom_point(data = sv, aes(X1, X2), shape = 21, size = 7, stroke = 1.2) +
  geom_point(data = moved[i, ], aes(X1, X2), shape = 4, size = 5, stroke = 2) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(`-1` = "#3B4992", `1` = "#EE0000"),
                      labels = c("y = -1", "y = +1"), name = NULL) +
  coord_equal(xlim = c(-0.5, 4.5), ylim = c(-0.5, 4.5), expand = FALSE) +
  labs(title = sprintf("Margin M = %.2f (was %.2f)   |   %d support vectors",
                       margin_M(m1), margin_M(m0), length(alphaindex(m1)[[1]])),
       subtitle = "x marks the point you are moving") +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

What you should see:

- **Far-away point:** slide it anywhere in its range — the hyperplane does not
  move at all. It is not a support vector, so it has no say.
- **Support vector, pulled toward the boundary** (negative): the margin
  shrinks immediately. The whole classifier is at the mercy of this one point.
- **Support vector, pushed away** (positive): the margin widens until another
  point takes over as a support vector.

That sensitivity is the maximal margin classifier's weakness, and the reason
the soft margin exists.

## 1.3 The soft margin: turning the cost dial

Now the classes overlap, so **no** separating hyperplane exists. The soft
margin lets some points sit inside the margin, or even on the wrong side of the
hyperplane. Slide the cost from cheap (left) to expensive (right).

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof log10C = Inputs.range([-2, 2], {value: 0, step: 0.25, label: "log₁₀(cost C)"})
```

```{webr}
#| autorun: true
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 6
#| input:
#|   - log10C
library(ggplot2)
library(kernlab)

set.seed(3)
n <- 50
ovl <- data.frame(X1 = c(rnorm(n, 1.2, 0.8), rnorm(n, 2.8, 0.8)),
                  X2 = c(rnorm(n, 1.2, 0.8), rnorm(n, 2.8, 0.8)),
                  y  = factor(rep(c(-1, 1), each = n)))

C <- 10^log10C
m <- ksvm(y ~ X1 + X2, data = ovl, kernel = "vanilladot", kpar = list(),
          C = C, scaled = FALSE)
w <- colSums(coef(m)[[1]] * xmatrix(m)[[1]])

grid <- expand.grid(X1 = seq(-1.5, 5.5, length.out = 150),
                    X2 = seq(-1.5, 5.5, length.out = 150))
grid$f <- predict(m, grid, type = "decision")[, 1]
sv <- ovl[alphaindex(m)[[1]], ]

ggplot() +
  geom_contour(data = grid, aes(X1, X2, z = f), breaks = 0,
               colour = "black", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_contour(data = grid, aes(X1, X2, z = f), breaks = c(-1, 1),
               colour = "black", linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_point(data = ovl, aes(X1, X2, colour = y), size = 2.5) +
  geom_point(data = sv, aes(X1, X2), shape = 21, size = 5, stroke = 0.8) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(`-1` = "#3B4992", `1` = "#EE0000"),
                      labels = c("y = -1", "y = +1"), name = NULL) +
  coord_equal(xlim = c(-1.5, 5.5), ylim = c(-1.5, 5.5), expand = FALSE) +
  labs(title = sprintf("cost C = %.2f   |   margin width = %.2f   |   %d support vectors   |   training error = %.0f%%",
                       C, 2 / sqrt(sum(w^2)), nSV(m), 100 * error(m))) +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom", plot.title = element_text(size = 11))
```

Sweep the slider end to end and watch three numbers move together:

| cost `C` | margin width | support vectors | training error |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0.01 (cheap violations) | 3.32 | 70 | 4% |
| 1 | 0.91 | 16 | 4% |
| 100 (expensive violations) | 0.59 | 10 | 3% |

- **Cheap violations → wide margin, many support vectors.** 70 of the 100
  points help set the boundary, so no single point can drag it around: **low
  variance, higher bias.**
- **Expensive violations → narrow margin, few support vectors.** The fit
  bends to a handful of points near the boundary: **low bias, higher
  variance.**
- **Training error barely changes (4% → 3%).** So training error cannot pick
  `C` for us — it will always favor expensive violations. We choose `C` the
  way we choose every tuning parameter: **cross-validation**. That is exactly
  what `caret::train()` does in Part 2.

## 1.4 Kernels: when a straight line won't do

Here class `+1` sits **inside** a ring and class `-1` outside it — no straight
line can separate them. We fit on 200 training points and report the error on
1,000 fresh test points from the same process. Try each kernel; for the
radial kernel, also slide $\gamma$ (kernlab calls it `sigma`).

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof kern = Inputs.select(["linear", "polynomial, degree 2", "polynomial, degree 3", "radial"], {value: "linear", label: "kernel"})
viewof log10gamma = Inputs.range([-1, 2], {value: 0, step: 0.25, label: "log₁₀(γ)  (radial only)"})
```

```{webr}
#| autorun: true
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 6
#| input:
#|   - kern
#|   - log10gamma
library(ggplot2)
library(kernlab)

make_ring <- function(n) {
  X1 <- runif(n, -2, 2)
  X2 <- runif(n, -2, 2)
  inside <- sqrt(X1^2 + X2^2) + rnorm(n, 0, 0.15) < 1.2
  data.frame(X1, X2, y = factor(ifelse(inside, 1, -1), levels = c(-1, 1)))
}
set.seed(4); ring_train <- make_ring(200)
set.seed(5); ring_test  <- make_ring(1000)

gamma <- 10^log10gamma
m <- switch(kern,
  "linear"               = ksvm(y ~ ., ring_train, kernel = "vanilladot",
                                kpar = list(), C = 1),
  "polynomial, degree 2" = ksvm(y ~ ., ring_train, kernel = "polydot",
                                kpar = list(degree = 2), C = 1),
  "polynomial, degree 3" = ksvm(y ~ ., ring_train, kernel = "polydot",
                                kpar = list(degree = 3), C = 1),
  "radial"               = ksvm(y ~ ., ring_train, kernel = "rbfdot",
                                kpar = list(sigma = gamma), C = 1))

train_err <- mean(predict(m, ring_train) != ring_train$y)
test_err  <- mean(predict(m, ring_test)  != ring_test$y)

grid <- expand.grid(X1 = seq(-2, 2, length.out = 150),
                    X2 = seq(-2, 2, length.out = 150))
grid$pred <- predict(m, grid)

ggplot() +
  geom_raster(data = grid, aes(X1, X2, fill = pred), alpha = 0.25) +
  geom_point(data = ring_train, aes(X1, X2, colour = y), size = 2) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(`-1` = "#3B4992", `1` = "#EE0000"),
                    guide = "none") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(`-1` = "#3B4992", `1` = "#EE0000"),
                      labels = c("y = -1 (outside)", "y = +1 (inside)"), name = NULL) +
  coord_equal(expand = FALSE) +
  labs(title = sprintf("%s%s   |   training error %.1f%%   |   test error %.1f%%",
                       kern, if (kern == "radial") sprintf(" (γ = %.2f)", gamma) else "",
                       100 * train_err, 100 * test_err)) +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom", plot.title = element_text(size = 11))
```

Things to try:

| kernel | training error | test error |
|---|---|---|
| linear | 30.5% | 28.5% |
| polynomial, degree 2 | 7.0% | 7.4% |
| radial, γ = 1 | 8.5% | 6.3% |
| radial, γ = 100 | 3.0% | 21.0% |

- **linear** gives up and calls everything "outside" — one straight cut can't
  carve out a disc, so it misclassifies the whole inside class.
- **polynomial, degree 2** gets close to the best possible: the true boundary
  $X_1^2 + X_2^2 = 1.2^2$ *is* a degree-2 curve. (Nothing reaches 0% — the
  labels near the ring are noisy on purpose.)
- **radial**, then slide $\gamma$ all the way right. The training error keeps
  falling while the test error climbs as the boundary shrink-wraps individual
  points. Large $\gamma$ = very local kernel = **overfitting**. $\gamma$ is a
  flexibility dial, just like $k$ in k-NN.

### Why the degree-2 kernel works: the enlarged feature space

The slides' trick was to add transformed features and fit a *linear*
classifier in the bigger space. Plot the same points on $X_1^2$ and $X_2^2$
instead of $X_1$ and $X_2$:

```{webr}
library(ggplot2)

set.seed(4)
X1 <- runif(200, -2, 2); X2 <- runif(200, -2, 2)
inside <- sqrt(X1^2 + X2^2) + rnorm(200, 0, 0.15) < 1.2
ring <- data.frame(X1sq = X1^2, X2sq = X2^2,
                   y = factor(ifelse(inside, 1, -1), levels = c(-1, 1)))

ggplot(ring, aes(X1sq, X2sq, colour = y)) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  geom_abline(intercept = 1.44, slope = -1, linetype = "dashed") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(`-1` = "#3B4992", `1` = "#EE0000"),
                      labels = c("y = -1 (outside)", "y = +1 (inside)"), name = NULL) +
  labs(x = expression(X[1]^2), y = expression(X[2]^2),
       title = "The ring becomes (almost) linearly separable",
       subtitle = "dashed line: X1² + X2² = 1.44") +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

In the transformed coordinates a straight line does the job. The polynomial
kernel gets the same result **without ever building those columns**: it only
needs inner products, which is what makes kernels cheap even when the enlarged
space is huge (or, for the radial kernel, infinite-dimensional).

# Part 2 — The tumor example from the slides

The slides motivated SVMs with benign vs. malignant tumors plotted on **cell
size uniformity** and **cell shape uniformity**. Those come from the Wisconsin
breast-cancer biopsy data, which ships with the `MASS` package as `biopsy`:
699 biopsies, nine cytology scores each rated 1–10, and the diagnosis.

```{webr}
library(MASS)
library(dplyr)

tumor <- biopsy |>
  na.omit() |>                      # 16 biopsies are missing bare_nuclei
  transmute(clump_thickness = V1, cell_size = V2, cell_shape = V3,
            adhesion = V4, epithelial_size = V5, bare_nuclei = V6,
            chromatin = V7, nucleoli = V8, mitoses = V9,
            class = factor(class, levels = c("benign", "malignant"),
                           labels = c("Benign", "Malignant")))

dim(tumor)
table(tumor$class)
```

683 complete biopsies, 65% benign. The scores are whole numbers from 1 to 10,
so many patients share exactly the same (size, shape) pair — we **jitter** the
points slightly so they don't stack on top of each other:

```{webr}
library(ggplot2)

ggplot(tumor, aes(cell_size, cell_shape, colour = class)) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.25, height = 0.25, size = 1.5, alpha = 0.6) +
  ggsci::scale_color_aaas() +
  labs(x = "Cell Size Uniformity", y = "Cell Shape Uniformity",
       colour = "Tumor Class",
       title = "Tumor classification based on biomarkers") +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

Mostly separable, with a band of overlap in the middle — a job for the soft
margin.

### Split, then tune the cost by cross-validation

```{webr}
library(caret)

set.seed(2155)
idx <- createDataPartition(tumor$class, p = 0.75, list = FALSE)
train_data <- tumor[idx, ]
test_data  <- tumor[-idx, ]

ctrl <- trainControl(method = "cv", number = 10)

set.seed(2155)
svm_2 <- train(class ~ cell_size + cell_shape, data = train_data,
               method = "svmLinear", trControl = ctrl,
               preProcess = c("center", "scale"),
               tuneGrid = expand.grid(C = 2^(-6:4)))

ggplot(svm_2$results, aes(C, Accuracy)) +
  geom_line() + geom_point() +
  scale_x_log10() +
  labs(x = "cost C (log scale)", y = "10-fold CV accuracy",
       title = "Cross-validated accuracy across the cost grid") +
  theme_bw()
svm_2$bestTune
```

Cross-validation picks `C = 8`, but look at the y-axis: accuracy only runs
from 0.934 to 0.951 across a 1,000-fold range of `C`. On this data the cost
barely matters. That is common — and it's why we tune on a log-spaced grid
rather than agonizing over one value.

### The fitted boundary

`predict()` on a grid of (size, shape) values paints the regions the SVM
assigns to each class. `caret` applies the same centering and scaling to the
grid that it applied to the training data.

```{webr}
grid <- expand.grid(cell_size  = seq(0.5, 10.5, length.out = 120),
                    cell_shape = seq(0.5, 10.5, length.out = 120))
grid$pred <- predict(svm_2, grid)

ggplot() +
  geom_raster(data = grid, aes(cell_size, cell_shape, fill = pred), alpha = 0.2) +
  geom_jitter(data = train_data, aes(cell_size, cell_shape, colour = class),
              width = 0.25, height = 0.25, size = 1.5, alpha = 0.6) +
  ggsci::scale_color_aaas() + ggsci::scale_fill_aaas(guide = "none") +
  labs(x = "Cell Size Uniformity", y = "Cell Shape Uniformity",
       colour = "Tumor Class", title = "Linear SVM on two biomarkers") +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

### How well does it do on the test set?

As in Lab 5 we set `positive = "Malignant"`, so **sensitivity** is the share of
cancers we catch.

```{webr}
confusionMatrix(predict(svm_2, test_data), test_data$class,
                positive = "Malignant")
```

With just two features the linear SVM gets **95.3%** of the 170 test biopsies
right, catching 56 of 59 cancers (sensitivity 0.949) while clearing 106 of 111
benign tumors (specificity 0.955).

### All nine features, three kernels

Now use every score, and compare the three kernels from class. All three go
through the same `train()` call; only `method` changes. **This is the heaviest
cell in Part 2** (the polynomial grid fits 270 models) — give it a moment.

```{webr}
f_all <- class ~ .

set.seed(2155)
svm_lin <- train(f_all, data = train_data, method = "svmLinear",
                 trControl = ctrl, preProcess = c("center", "scale"),
                 tuneGrid = expand.grid(C = 2^(-6:4)))
set.seed(2155)
svm_poly <- train(f_all, data = train_data, method = "svmPoly",
                  trControl = ctrl, preProcess = c("center", "scale"),
                  tuneLength = 3)
set.seed(2155)
svm_rad <- train(f_all, data = train_data, method = "svmRadial",
                 trControl = ctrl, preProcess = c("center", "scale"),
                 tuneLength = 6)

summarise_svm <- function(model, name) {
  cm <- confusionMatrix(predict(model, test_data), test_data$class,
                        positive = "Malignant")
  data.frame(Model = name,
             Accuracy    = round(cm$overall[["Accuracy"]], 3),
             Sensitivity = round(cm$byClass[["Sensitivity"]], 3),
             Specificity = round(cm$byClass[["Specificity"]], 3))
}

rbind(summarise_svm(svm_2,    "Linear, 2 features"),
      summarise_svm(svm_lin,  "Linear, 9 features"),
      summarise_svm(svm_poly, "Polynomial, 9 features"),
      summarise_svm(svm_rad,  "Radial, 9 features"))
```

- **More features help:** going from two scores to nine lifts accuracy from
  0.953 to 0.971 and sensitivity from 0.949 to 0.983 (one missed cancer instead
  of three).
- **More flexible kernels don't:** linear, polynomial, and radial land within
  one test biopsy of each other. Cross-validation even picked the *smallest*
  cost on the grid for the linear kernel — the widest, most forgiving margin.
- The lesson from §1.4 in reverse: a kernel only pays off when the true boundary
  is curved. These cytology scores rise together as a tumor turns malignant,
  so a straight cut is already about as good as it gets. Try the linear kernel
  first; reach for a kernel only when CV says it helps.

# Part 3 — More than two classes

SVMs are binary by construction. The slides gave two ways round that:
**one-versus-all** (fit $K$ classifiers, each class against the rest) and
**one-versus-one** (fit all $\binom{K}{2}$ pairwise classifiers and let them
vote). `kernlab` uses **one-versus-one**. With three iris species that means
$\binom{3}{2} = 3$ binary SVMs inside one fitted model — we can count them:

```{webr}
library(kernlab)

set.seed(1)
m_iris <- ksvm(Species ~ ., data = iris, kernel = "rbfdot")
length(coef(m_iris))   # one set of coefficients per pairwise classifier
```

The interactive plot below shows the combined vote as three-colored decision
regions. The two feature pairs give very different problems:

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof iris_features = Inputs.radio(["petal", "sepal"], {value: "petal", label: "features"})
viewof iris_kernel = Inputs.radio(["linear", "radial"], {value: "linear", label: "kernel"})
```

```{webr}
#| autorun: true
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 6
#| input:
#|   - iris_features
#|   - iris_kernel
library(ggplot2)
library(kernlab)

vars <- if (iris_features == "petal") c("Petal.Length", "Petal.Width") else
                                      c("Sepal.Length", "Sepal.Width")
d <- data.frame(x1 = iris[[vars[1]]], x2 = iris[[vars[2]]], Species = iris$Species)

set.seed(1)
m <- if (iris_kernel == "linear") {
  ksvm(Species ~ x1 + x2, data = d, kernel = "vanilladot", kpar = list(),
       C = 1, cross = 10)
} else {
  ksvm(Species ~ x1 + x2, data = d, kernel = "rbfdot", C = 1, cross = 10)
}

grid <- expand.grid(x1 = seq(min(d$x1) - 0.3, max(d$x1) + 0.3, length.out = 150),
                    x2 = seq(min(d$x2) - 0.3, max(d$x2) + 0.3, length.out = 150))
grid$pred <- predict(m, grid)

ggplot() +
  geom_raster(data = grid, aes(x1, x2, fill = pred), alpha = 0.25) +
  geom_jitter(data = d, aes(x1, x2, colour = Species, shape = Species),
              width = 0.03, height = 0.03, size = 2.5) +
  ggsci::scale_color_aaas() + ggsci::scale_fill_aaas(guide = "none") +
  coord_cartesian(expand = FALSE) +
  labs(x = vars[1], y = vars[2],
       title = sprintf("%s kernel on %s features   |   10-fold CV error %.1f%%",
                       iris_kernel, iris_features, 100 * cross(m))) +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

- **Petal features:** both kernels separate the three species almost perfectly
  (10-fold CV error 4.7% linear, 4.0% radial). Setosa sits far off on its own;
  the two classifiers that involve it are easy.
- **Sepal features:** the error jumps to about 21% (linear) and 25% (radial).
  Versicolor and virginica overlap heavily on sepal measurements, and no
  kernel can separate points that sit on top of each other — the radial kernel
  just draws a more contorted boundary through the overlap and does *worse*.
  Better features beat a fancier kernel.

# Part 4 — Variable selection for classification

Everything so far used a few hand-picked features. Real problems often come
with many correlated candidates, and we would like the data to tell us which
ones matter. Back to the **Wisconsin Diagnostic (WDBC)** data from Lab 5, this
time with **all 30 features**: ten nuclear measurements, each recorded as a
mean, a standard error, and a "worst" value.

```{webr}
library(dplyr)
library(caret)

wdbc <- read.csv("data/wdbc.csv") |>
  mutate(diagnosis = factor(diagnosis, levels = c("B", "M"),
                            labels = c("Benign", "Malignant")))

set.seed(2155)
idx <- createDataPartition(wdbc$diagnosis, p = 0.75, list = FALSE)
wtrain <- wdbc[idx, ]
wtest  <- wdbc[-idx, ]

c(train = nrow(wtrain), test = nrow(wtest), features = ncol(wdbc) - 1)
```

### Why not just throw everything into logistic regression?

```{webr}
full_glm <- glm(diagnosis ~ ., data = wtrain, family = binomial)
summary(abs(coef(full_glm)))
```

R warns that the algorithm **did not converge** and that fitted probabilities
are **numerically 0 or 1**. The training tumors are perfectly separable in 30
dimensions, so the likelihood keeps improving as the coefficients grow —
the median coefficient is about 500 and the largest about 44,000, on the
log-odds scale. These estimates mean nothing, and
(spoiler) the model does worst of everything we'll try on the test set.

### The lasso: logistic regression with a penalty

The fix is the same one we used for regression in [Lab 3](../../03-regression-1/code/class3_lab1.html): add a penalty. The
**lasso** maximizes

$$\underbrace{\sum_{i=1}^n \log L(\beta;\, y_i, x_i)}_{\text{logistic log-likelihood}} \; - \; \lambda \sum_{j=1}^{p} |\beta_j| .$$

The absolute-value penalty does two jobs at once: it keeps the coefficients
finite, and it sets many of them **exactly to zero** — so fitting the model
*is* selecting variables. $\lambda$ controls how many survive. `glmnet` fits
the whole path of $\lambda$ values in one call (`alpha = 1` is the lasso;
`alpha = 0` would be ridge).

The features are on very different scales (areas in the hundreds,
smoothness around 0.1), and the penalty treats every $\beta_j$ alike, so we
**standardize first**, using the training means and SDs for both sets.

```{webr}
library(glmnet)

X_train <- scale(as.matrix(wtrain[, -1]))
X_test  <- scale(as.matrix(wtest[, -1]),
                 center = attr(X_train, "scaled:center"),
                 scale  = attr(X_train, "scaled:scale"))

lasso_path <- glmnet(X_train, wtrain$diagnosis, family = "binomial", alpha = 1)
plot(lasso_path, xvar = "lambda", label = TRUE)
```

Read the plot right to left: at large $\lambda$ (right) every coefficient is
zero; as $\lambda$ shrinks, features enter one at a time. The numbers along
the top count how many are in the model.

### Pick your own λ

Slide $\lambda$ and watch which features survive and how the test accuracy
responds.

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof log10lambda = Inputs.range([-3.5, -0.5], {value: -1, step: 0.1, label: "log₁₀(λ)"})
```

```{webr}
#| autorun: true
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 6
#| input:
#|   - log10lambda
library(ggplot2)
library(glmnet)
library(caret)

wd <- read.csv("data/wdbc.csv")
wd$diagnosis <- factor(wd$diagnosis, levels = c("B", "M"),
                       labels = c("Benign", "Malignant"))
set.seed(2155)
ix <- createDataPartition(wd$diagnosis, p = 0.75, list = FALSE)
Xtr <- scale(as.matrix(wd[ix, -1]))
Xte <- scale(as.matrix(wd[-ix, -1]), center = attr(Xtr, "scaled:center"),
             scale = attr(Xtr, "scaled:scale"))

lam <- 10^log10lambda
fit <- glmnet(Xtr, wd$diagnosis[ix], family = "binomial", alpha = 1)
b   <- as.matrix(coef(fit, s = lam))[-1, 1]
b   <- b[b != 0]
acc <- mean(predict(fit, Xte, s = lam, type = "class") == wd$diagnosis[-ix])

if (length(b) == 0) {
  b <- c("(no features selected)" = 0)
}
coefs <- data.frame(feature = names(b), beta = unname(b))
coefs$effect <- factor(ifelse(coefs$beta > 0, "raises P(Malignant)",
                              "lowers P(Malignant)"),
                       levels = c("lowers P(Malignant)", "raises P(Malignant)"))

ggplot(coefs, aes(beta, reorder(feature, abs(beta)), fill = effect)) +
  geom_col() +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("lowers P(Malignant)" = "#3B4992",
                               "raises P(Malignant)" = "#EE0000"),
                    name = NULL, drop = FALSE) +
  labs(x = "standardized coefficient", y = NULL,
       title = sprintf("λ = %.4f   |   %d of 30 features kept   |   test accuracy %.1f%%",
                       lam, sum(coefs$beta != 0), 100 * acc)) +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

A few settings to try:

| log₁₀(λ) | features kept | test accuracy |
|---|---|---|
| −3.5 | 21 | 97.9% |
| −2.0 | 8 | 97.9% |
| −1.0 | 4 | 95.1% |
| −0.5 | 2 | 69.7% |

From 21 features down to 8 the test accuracy **does not move**: those extra
13 features were redundant. Around 6 features it starts to slip, and at
2 the model has thrown away real signal. Somewhere in between is the smallest
model that is still as good as the big one — which is what cross-validation
will find.

### Letting cross-validation choose λ

`cv.glmnet()` runs 10-fold CV along the whole path. It reports two choices:
`lambda.min` (the lowest CV error) and `lambda.1se` (the largest $\lambda$
within one standard error of that minimum — the simplest model that is
statistically as good). For selection we usually prefer `lambda.1se`.

```{webr}
set.seed(2155)
lasso_cv <- cv.glmnet(X_train, wtrain$diagnosis, family = "binomial",
                      alpha = 1, nfolds = 10)
plot(lasso_cv)

b_1se <- coef(lasso_cv, s = "lambda.1se")
selected <- rownames(b_1se)[b_1se[, 1] != 0][-1]   # drop the intercept
selected
```

The `lambda.1se` model keeps **10 of the 30 features**. Notice what's
there: mostly **"worst"** measurements (the most abnormal cells in the image)
and the **concavity / concave points** family — the irregular, indented cell
outlines a pathologist looks for. Of radius, perimeter, and area — three
near-copies of "how big is the nucleus" — the lasso keeps area_worst and
radius_worst but not perimeter: with correlated features, the lasso tends to
keep one or two representatives and drop the rest.

### Does selecting features cost us anything?

Compare, on the same 142 test tumors: the unpenalized logistic model, the
lasso, ridge (penalized but no selection), and a linear SVM trained on all 30
features vs. only the lasso's picks.

```{webr}
set.seed(2155)
ridge_cv <- cv.glmnet(X_train, wtrain$diagnosis, family = "binomial",
                      alpha = 0, nfolds = 10)

set.seed(2155)
svm_all <- train(X_train, wtrain$diagnosis, method = "svmLinear",
                 trControl = trainControl(method = "cv", number = 10),
                 tuneGrid = expand.grid(C = 2^(-6:4)))
set.seed(2155)
svm_sel <- train(X_train[, selected], wtrain$diagnosis, method = "svmLinear",
                 trControl = trainControl(method = "cv", number = 10),
                 tuneGrid = expand.grid(C = 2^(-6:4)))

glm_pred <- ifelse(predict(full_glm, wtest, type = "response") > 0.5,
                   "Malignant", "Benign")
acc <- function(pred) round(mean(pred == wtest$diagnosis), 3)

data.frame(
  Model = c("Logistic, no penalty", "Lasso logistic (lambda.1se)",
            "Ridge logistic (lambda.1se)", "Linear SVM, all features",
            "Linear SVM, lasso-selected features"),
  Features = c(30, length(selected), 30, 30, length(selected)),
  Test_accuracy = c(acc(glm_pred),
                    acc(predict(lasso_cv, X_test, s = "lambda.1se", type = "class")),
                    acc(predict(ridge_cv, X_test, s = "lambda.1se", type = "class")),
                    acc(predict(svm_all, X_test)),
                    acc(predict(svm_sel, X_test[, selected])))
)
```

- **The unpenalized model is worst (0.944)** — the inflated coefficients from
  above do real damage on new data.
- **Lasso with 10 features = ridge with 30 = SVM with 30 (all 0.979).** We got
  a model a third the size at no cost in accuracy, and one that names which
  measurements matter.
- **The SVM on the lasso's 10 features is one tumor behind (0.972).** Variable
  selection by one method can be handed to another.
- Everything — the standardization, the λ choice, the selected list — came from
  the **training** tumors only. Selecting features on all the data and then
  "testing" on part of it leaks information and makes the test accuracy look
  better than it is.

### How stable is the selection?

The lasso's choice depends on the data it saw — including the random
assignment of CV folds. Re-run the CV with 10 different fold assignments and
count how often each feature is picked. To keep it quick we search a 30-point
λ grid around where `lambda.1se` landed. **This is the slowest cell in the
lab** — allow up to a minute.

```{webr}
#| timelimit: 300
lambda_grid <- 10^seq(-1, -3, length.out = 30)

picks <- sapply(1:10, function(s) {
  set.seed(s)
  cvfit <- cv.glmnet(X_train, wtrain$diagnosis, family = "binomial",
                     alpha = 1, nfolds = 10, lambda = lambda_grid)
  as.matrix(coef(cvfit, s = "lambda.1se"))[-1, 1] != 0
})

freq <- sort(rowMeans(picks), decreasing = TRUE)
freq <- freq[freq > 0]

ggplot(data.frame(feature = names(freq), freq = freq),
       aes(freq, reorder(feature, freq))) +
  geom_col(fill = "#3B4992") +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  labs(x = "share of 10 CV runs that selected the feature", y = NULL,
       title = "Lasso selection frequency across CV fold assignments") +
  theme_bw()
```

Seven features are chosen in **every** run — concavity_mean,
concave_points_mean, radius_worst, texture_worst, smoothness_worst,
concave_points_worst, symmetry_worst. Those you can trust. The rest come and
go with nothing more than a reshuffle of the CV folds (area_worst, picked in our
single run above, rarely or never makes the cut here). A single lasso fit gives one
list; a stability check tells you which parts of it are real. Report the
stable core, not whatever one run happened to say.

### A connection worth knowing

The SVM is secretly a penalized method too. ISLR §9.5 shows the support vector
classifier solves

$$\min_{\beta}\; \sum_{i=1}^n \max\big[0,\, 1 - y_i f(x_i)\big] \;+\; \lambda \sum_{j=1}^p \beta_j^2 ,$$

a **hinge loss** plus a **ridge** penalty — and $\lambda$ plays the role of
$1/C$ for the software cost. Swap the hinge loss for the logistic loss and you
have ridge logistic regression; swap the ridge penalty for the lasso penalty
and you have the lasso. "Regularization for classification" is one recipe —
**loss + penalty** — with interchangeable parts.

## Try it yourself

**1. Elastic net.** `alpha` between 0 and 1 mixes the lasso and ridge
penalties. Correlated features (radius, perimeter, and area are nearly the
same measurement) tend to enter *together* under the elastic net, where the
lasso picks one and drops the rest. Fill in an `alpha` and compare how many
features survive — and whether the test accuracy changes at all.

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_enet
set.seed(2155)
enet_cv <- cv.glmnet(X_train, wtrain$diagnosis, family = "binomial",
                     alpha = ______, nfolds = 10)   # try 0.5, then 0.1

b <- coef(enet_cv, s = "lambda.1se")
c(features_kept = sum(b[-1, 1] != 0),
  test_accuracy = mean(predict(enet_cv, X_test, s = "lambda.1se",
                               type = "class") == wtest$diagnosis))
```

**2. A different split.** In Part 2, change `set.seed(2155)` before
`createDataPartition()` to another number and re-run the part. Does the
linear kernel still hold its own against the radial one?

**3. Break the ring.** In §1.4, the ring's noise is `rnorm(n, 0, 0.15)`.
There is no slider for it — edit the cell, raise it to `0.4`, and re-run. What
happens to the test error of the degree-2 kernel, and why can no kernel fix
it?

## Things worth remembering

- **The margin is decided by a few points.** Only the support vectors shape the
  SVM; everything else could move (within limits) without changing the fit.
- **Cost `C` in software is the opposite of the budget $C$ on the slides.**
  Large software `C` = expensive violations = narrow margin = low bias, high
  variance. Tune it by cross-validation, never by training error.
- **Kernels buy flexibility, and flexibility has to be earned.** On the ring a
  degree-2 kernel is exactly right; on the tumor data a straight line is
  already as good as anything fancier.
- **Multi-class SVMs are a vote.** `kernlab` fits one binary SVM per pair of
  classes.
- **With many correlated features, penalize.** Unpenalized logistic regression
  broke on 30 correlated features; the lasso kept the coefficients sane *and*
  selected a short list — but check how stable that list is before you
  interpret it.
